paper_title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Spoken dialogue models (SDMs) enable end-toend speech interaction by modeling speech input and generating text tokens together with speech tokens, which are then synthesized into waveforms by speech decoder (Défossez et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a; KimiTeam et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Existing SDMs typically use the same token space for autoregressive generation and speech synthesis, tightly coupling generation with the representation required by the speech *Corresponding author. 1Code: https://github.com/yingzhuodeng/CoSTA 1 Figure 1: Overview of CoSTA. Existing SDMs couple generation and synthesis token spaces. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations and deterministically expands them back to the original space before synthesis. decoder. These speech-token sequences are often overly long, increasing autoregressive generation cost, complicating text-speech alignment, and making long-context speech modeling more difficult (Shen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). In practical interaction, this inefficiency slows responses and consumes generation budgets faster, limiting sustained interaction and spoken-response duration. One solution is to design speech tokenizers with lower token rates (Défossez et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025c; Guo et al., 2026). However, aggressive rate reduction may introduce compressionquality trade-off, and replacing the tokenizer of an existing SDM may require retraining or adapting the tokenizer, paired speech decoder, and SDM together. More fundamentally, this route still couples generation and synthesis to the same representation. We therefore ask different question: Can we decouple the token space used for autoregressive generation from that required for speech synthesis, while preserving the original speech tokenizer and decoder? Speech-token sequences produced by existing tokenizers exhibit substantial redundancy and can be losslessly compressed using BPE (Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016; Radford et al., 2019). Across diverse tokenizer, data, and language settings, we uncover an empirical scaling regularity: BPE compression shortens speech-token sequences with increasing vocabulary size, following an approximate log-linear trend on held-out speech. This persistent compressibility suggests route to more efficient generation without altering synthesis: using compact autoregressive representation while deterministically recovering the original speech-token sequence required by the decoder. This insight motivates generationsynthesis token-space decoupling and CoSTA, short for Compressed Speech Token Adaptation, compatibility-preserving post-hoc token-space adaptation framework for existing large-scale SDMs. As illustrated in Figure 1, CoSTA extends the autoregressive generation token space with compressed representations while preserving the original synthesis interface. CoSTA adapts the SDM to generate these compressed representations through vocabulary extension with mean initialization, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation. At inference time, generated compressed units are deterministically expanded back to the original speech-token representations before synthesis, reducing autoregressive speech-token steps while leaving the original speech tokenizer and decoder unchanged. We validate CoSTA on two representative SDM architectures. In experiments with Step-Audio 2 mini (Wu et al., 2025), CoSTA achieves 1.736 and 1.659 relative expanded speech-token generation speed in Chinese and English, respectively, while preserving response quality according to both automatic and human evaluations. These gains further translate into lower full-response latency, higher throughput, and more sustained interaction under limited budgets. Vocabulary scaling further reveals practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and response quality. Experiments on different SDM architecture further demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate speech tokenization. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We uncover an approximate log-linear scaling regularity of speech-token compression over 10K320K added units across eight tokenizer configurations, data sources, and languages. We formulate generationsynthesis tokenspace decoupling and introduce CoSTA, compatibility-preserving post-hoc adaptation Figure 2: Speech-token BPE scaling across eight tokenizer configurations. Compression rate decreases approximately linearly with log2 vocabulary size. framework that enables existing SDMs to generate compact, losslessly expandable speechtoken sequences while retaining their original speech tokenizer and decoder. We demonstrate that CoSTA improves modelside and system efficiency while preserving response quality, with additional evidence of cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate speech tokenization. We further characterize compressed-token generation: CoSTA enables more sustained interaction under limited budgets, while vocabulary scaling reveals practical trade-off among compression, efficiency, and quality.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Section 2 motivates generationsynthesis tokenspace decoupling. Realizing this decoupling in an existing SDM, however, requires adapting the model while preserving compatibility with its original tokenizerdecoder pipeline. We therefore propose CoSTA, compatibility-preserving post-hoc token-space adaptation framework. CoSTA adapts the SDM to generate compressed sequences in the extended token space Z, while deterministic expansion π(z) = restores the original decoder-facing representation in before waveform synthesis. As shown in Figure 3, CoSTA consists of three steps: (1) vocabulary extension with mean-based initialization, (2) pronunciation adaptation on compressed TTS data, and (3) dialogue adaptation on compressed speech-to-speech dialogue data. At inference time, only lightweight deterministic BPE expansion is inserted before the unchanged speech decoder. We detail each step below.

sections.title: 3.2 Pronunciation Adaptation
sections.content: After vocabulary extension, the SDM has an extended generation token space but has not yet learned to use the added BPE units reliably. We therefore perform pronunciation adaptation on compressed TTS data. Following interleavedgeneration SDMs such as Step-Audio 2 mini (Wu et al., 2025), each target sequence contains both text and speech tokens. We apply BPE compression only to speech tokens and leave text tokens unchanged. Each example consists of text prompt and target response sequence y, where contains interleaved text tokens and original speech tokens. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Implementation. We use the 8B Step-Audio 2 mini (Wu et al., 2025) as the SDM for its strong open-source support, simple architecture, and competitive dialogue performance; it uses S3Tokenizer V2 at 25 Hz. For pronunciation adaptation, we sample 300 hours each of Chinese and English speech from Emilia (He et al., 2024) and convert them to unified timbre with Seed-VC (Liu, 2024). For dialogue adaptation, we follow OpenS2S (Wang et al., 2025a) to construct approximately 50K speechdialogue examples per language, with assistant speech synthesized by CosyVoice 2 (Du et al., 2024b) using consistent voice. We learn the BPE vocabulary from dialogue speech-token sequences and use 80K added units, supported by the vocabulary-size trade-off analysis in Section 4.4. Vocabulary extension adds only embedding and LM-head rows, about 6% of the original model parameters. We train CoSTA-ZH, CoSTA-EN, and CoSTA-MIX for Chinese, English, and bilingual adaptation; further training details and data statistics are provided in Appendices and B.1. Baselines and benchmarks. We compare against the original Step-Audio 2 mini and VanillaFT-ZH/EN/MIX, which use the same adaptation data and training configuration while retaining the original speech tokens. This controls for training-data scale and isolates the effect of BPEcompressed token adaptation. Qwen2.5-Omni (Xu et al., 2025a), Kimi-Audio (KimiTeam et al., 2025), and GLM-4-Voice (Zeng et al., 2024) serve as external quality references. We evaluate on 12 datasets from URO-Bench (Yan et al., 2025), covering aligned Chinese and English settings and spanning summarization, mathematical and common-sense reasoning, open-ended dialogue, and real-world conversation, providing broad coverage of realistic spoken-dialogue scenarios. Efficiency metrics. We report three model-side efficiency metrics. First, the generated-token compression rate ρg = ρ((cid:98)z) is computed using Eq. 1, where (cid:98)z denotes the model-generated speech-token sequence; lower ρg indicates fewer autoregressive speech-token steps. Second, the expanded speech-token generation speed is Speed = π((cid:98)z) Tdecode , (7) where Tdecode is LLM decoding time, measuring the effective number of original speech tokens generated per second after expansion. System efficiency. Table 2 shows that decoding gains translate into lower full-response latency and higher throughput. Relative to the base model, CoSTA reduces latency by 32.839.0% in Chinese and 22.426.0% in English across the tested concurrency levels; throughput increases by 51.659.2% and 25.838.6%, respectively. It also outperforms matched Vanilla-FT at every tested setting, with at most 0.68 GiB additional peak memory. These workload-level results show that CoSTAs modelside efficiency gains translate into system-level improvements in latency and throughput with minimal memory overhead. Model-side efficiency. Table 1 shows substantial efficiency gains in both languages under the vLLM streaming inference setting. CoSTA-ZH reaches ρg = 66.81% and 1.736 relative speed, while CoSTA-EN reaches 70.17% and 1.659. CoSTAMIX shows similar improvements, whereas vanilla fine-tuning retains ρg = 100% with nearly unchanged generation speed. These results show that compressed-token modeling reduces autoregressive speech-token steps and translates this reduction into higher generation efficiency. Automatic quality evaluation. sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: Table 4 shows that the adaptation components play complementary roles. Timbre conversion mainly benefits response quality, while progressive adaptation modestly improves compressed-token generation. Pronunciation adaptation further strengthens compression and text-speech alignment, supporting reliable generation in the extended token space. Dialogue adaptation has the largest effect: removing it causes G-Eval to drop sharply from 72.27 to 24.35, indicating that learning compressed pronunciation alone is insufficient to recover spoken-dialogue capability. Appendix C.8 further analyzes the associated compressed-token behavior and response failures. Figures 6 and 8 further show that mean initialization provides faster convergence and more stable gradients than the alternatives; detailed initialization strategies are described in Appendix C.2.

sections.content: Discrete speech tokens. Discrete speech tokens include acoustic tokens from codec models (Zeghidour et al., 2022; Défossez et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024) and semantic tokens from discriminative (Du et al., 2024a,b, 2025) or self-supervised speech models (Baevski et al., 2020a,b; Hsu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2021). Lower-rate tokenizers shorten speech-token sequences (Défossez et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025c; Guo et al., 2026), but aggressive rate reduction may introduce compressionquality trade-offs, while tokenizer replacement may require retraining or adapting the tokenizer, speech decoder, and SDM together. Moreover, this approach still couples generation and synthesis to the same token space. Acoustic-piece and BPE methods have been explored in ASR (Ren et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2023, 2024), speech continuation (Shen et al., 2024), and TTS (Zhu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), primarily through native training of small, task-specific models. In contrast, CoSTA enables post-hoc adaptation of existing large-scale SDMs for efficient compressed-token generation. We further uncover consistent scaling regularity of speech-token compression and characterize the vocabulary-size trade-off. 6 Conclusion We uncover an approximate log-linear scaling regularity in speech-token BPE and introduce CoSTA, which decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA achieves approximately 1.7 expanded speech-token generation speed and improves system efficiency while preserving response quality. It also supports more sustained interaction, reveals vocabulary-size trade-offs, and transfers across SDM architectures, complementing low-rate tokenization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: This work has several limitations and possible extensions. First, our dialogue-adaptation data is constructed from synthesized speech-to-speech examples. While such data provides controllable and consistent speech responses for studying speechtoken compression, it is also practical and widely adopted choice for training spoken dialogue models, as large-scale, high-quality real speech-tospeech dialogue data is difficult to collect. Future work may further explore how synthetic and real conversational speech data complement each other. Second, we adopt BPE as deterministic, lossless, and easily integrated compression method. Future work may investigate other lossless speech-token segmentation strategies and compare their behavior in spoken dialogue modeling. Finally, our evaluation focuses on general speech-to-speech dialogue and efficiency. Future work may extend the analysis to finer-grained scenarios, such as emotional dialogue, personalized speaking styles, and diverse acoustic environments.

sections.title: Hyperparameters
sections.content: This section reports the implementation details and hyperparameters used in CoSTA. Unless otherwise specified, all models are initialized from Step-Audio 2 mini (Wu et al., 2025). The original speech tokenizer and speech decoder are kept unchanged throughout all experiments. The original speech-token vocabulary contains 6,656 tokens. We train the BPE tokenizer using the HuggingFace tokenizers library2 on speech-token sequences extracted from the general speech-to-speech dialogue corpus, and extend the original vocabulary with 80K additional BPE speech tokens. Since the BPE trainer does not directly operate on integervalued speech-token sequences, we map each original speech-token ID to unique Unicode character before BPE training. During BPE expansion, generated BPE-token IDs are first converted into their corresponding Unicode strings, and BPE expansion is performed in the Unicode space; the resulting BPE-expanded Unicode sequence is then mapped back to the corresponding original speechtoken IDs. This conversion is deterministic and does not change the underlying speech-token sequence. All adaptation and inference experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. For all adaptation stages, we use the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), train with bfloat16 mixed precision (Micikevicius et al., 2018; Kalamkar et al., 2019), and use DeepSpeed (Rasley et al., 2020) with ZeRO-1 optimizer-state partitioning (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) for distributed training. A.1 Pronunciation Adaptation Pronunciation adaptation is conducted on compressed general TTS data. Following the progressive adaptation strategy, we split the pronunciationadaptation data into two halves. In the first stage, only the embedding and LM head layers of the vocabulary-extended model are updated. We use relatively large learning rate of 1.6 104 in this stage, which leads to faster loss reduction and more stable optimization as shown in Figures 6 and 8. In the second stage, intermediate model layers are further unfrozen and trained with smaller learning rate of 2.0 105 to complete pronunciation adaptation. sections.title: B Training Data and Benchmarks
sections.content: This section provides additional details about the training data and evaluation benchmarks used in our experiments. B.1 Training Data Pronunciation-adaptation data. For pronunciation adaptation, we use Emilia (He et al., 2024), large-scale multilingual speech generation dataset constructed from in-the-wild speech. Emilia contains diverse speech data across multiple languages and speaking styles, making it suitable for training speech generation models. In this work, we sample 300 hours of Chinese speech and 300 hours of English speech from Emilia. To reduce speaker variation and improve speech-token pattern consistency, we convert the sampled utterances into unified timbre using Seed-VC (Liu, 2024). The converted speech is then tokenized by the original speech tokenizer of Step-Audio 2 mini (Wu et al., 2025), and the resulting speech tokens are compressed with the learned BPE tokenizer. Text tokens remain unchanged. Specifically, we first collect general text instructions from InstructS2S-200K (Fang et al., 2025a) and translate the English instructions into Chinese using Qwen332B (Yang et al., 2025), yielding bilingual text instructions. We then select seed audio with neutral emotion labels and convert these text instructions into user speech queries. Following the speech response generation process in OpenS2S, Qwen332B is used to generate dialogue-appropriate text responses, and CosyVoice 2 (Du et al., 2024b) synthesizes the corresponding assistant speech with consistent reference voice. Following this pipeline, we initially construct 50K Chinese and 50K English general speech-to-speech instruction examples, each containing users speech query and an assistant response. We further filter out examples whose query or response speech exceeds one minute, resulting in 49,664 Chinese and 49,408 English dialogue examples. The statistics of the training data are summarized in Table 10. During training, only speech tokens in the target response are BPE-compressed, while text tokens remain unchanged. The compressed speech tokens are arranged according to the original text-speech interleaving pattern used by the base SDM. B.2 Evaluation Benchmarks prompt_open We evaluate models on URO-Bench (Yan et al., 2025), comprehensive benchmark for end-to-end spoken dialogue models in speech-to-speech scenarios. URO-Bench covers three major evaluation dimensions: Understanding, Reasoning, and Oral Conversation, and assesses not only responsecontent quality but also speech quality and speechtext alignment. In our experiments, we use 12 aligned Chinese and English datasets from UROBench, as summarized in Table 11. These benchmarks better reflect realistic spoken dialogue scenarios, making them well aligned with our goal of improving the efficiency and usability of speechto-speech SDMs. Following the URO-Bench evaluation protocol, we evaluate output quality using its prompts and scoring procedures. Specifically, we report the following metrics: (1) G-Eval measures response-content quality by transcribing the generated speech with an ASR model and prompting GPT-4o mini (OpenAI, 2024) to score the transcription. We use Whisper-large-v3 (Radford et al., 2023) for English transcription and Paraformer-zh (Gao et al., 2022) for Chinese transcription. (2) UTMOS (Saeki et al., 2022) estimates speech quality with predicted mean opinion score that reflects clarity, naturalness, and fluency. (3) WER/CER evaluates the alignment between the speech and text outputs of SDMs by computing the Word Error Rate (WER) or Character Error Rate (CER) between the generated text and the transcription of the generated speech. URO-Bench uses different evaluation prompts according to the task format. For open-ended tasks, including AlpacaEval-zh, AlpacaEval, Claude-zh, CommonEval, Wildchat-zh, and WildchatEval, we use prompt_open. For semi-open tasks with reference answers, including LCSTS-zh and Summary, we use prompt_semi_open. For questionanswering tasks with deterministic references, including APE-zh, Gsm8kEval, MLC-zh, and MLC, we use prompt_qa. These prompts are fed into GPT-4o mini together with the user instruction, the model response, and reference answer when available, to obtain the final G-Eval score. sections.content: This section provides detailed quality results, initialization and data-scaling analyses, compression across corpus settings, first-packet latency, human evaluation, OpenS2S transfer, and vocabulary-size and adaptation analyses. C.1 Detailed Main Results In the main paper, we report per-dataset G-Eval scores and average ASR-CER/WER and UTMOS results for Chinese and English URO-Bench datasets. To provide more complete comparison, Tables 14 and 15 further report the detailed values of all metrics on each dataset, including G-Eval, ASR-CER/WER, and UTMOS. These results detail the average quality trends discussed in the main paper and the variation across tasks; improvements are not uniform for every metric and dataset. C.

sections.title: Initialization Strategy Analysis
sections.content: Initialization strategies. We compare three strategies for initializing the embedding and LMhead rows of newly added BPE units. Random initialization initializes the new rows randomly, without using their constituent original speech tokens. Select initialization copies the embedding and LM-head row of one randomly selected token from the deterministic original-token expansion 16 Figure 8: Gradient norm during the first stage of pronunciation adaptation. Mean initialization yields more stable optimization than the alternatives. Figure 9: Held-out compression across data sources and languages with S3Tokenizer V2. Points are test measurements; lines are fits against log added vocabulary size. Emilia-TC denotes timbre-converted Emilia. of each BPE unit. Mean initialization, used by CoSTA, averages the corresponding rows of all constituent tokens as defined in Eq. 4. We evaluate these strategies with learning rates of 2 105 and 1.6 104 during the first phase of pronunciation adaptation. Figures 6 and 8 show that mean initialization converges faster and maintains more stable gradients than the alternatives, particularly at the larger learning rate. This suggests that aggregating the constituent originaltoken representations provides better starting point for adapting the newly added BPE units. C.3 Data Scaling Analysis We further analyze how the amount of adaptation data affects CoSTA. These scaling experiments were conducted in an early setting without progressive adaptation, and were mainly evaluated on four Chinese URO-Bench datasets: AlpacaEvalzh, APE-zh, Claude-zh, and MLC-zh. We study two scaling settings: varying the amount of pronunciation-adaptation data while keeping the dialogue-adaptation data fixed, and varying the amount of dialogue-adaptation data while keeping the pronunciation-adaptation data fixed. Scaling pronunciation-adaptation data. Table 16 reports the results when varying the amount of TTS data used for pronunciation adaptation, while fixing the dialogue-adaptation data to 50K examples. Increasing the amount of TTS data generally improves compressed-token learning, especially in terms of compression rate and speech-text alignment. However, the improvement becomes less pronounced as the TTS data size continues to increase. This suggests that pronunciation adaptation benefits from sufficient TTS data, while the marginal gain becomes smaller beyond certain scale. Based on this trade-off, we use 300h TTS data as the default setting, which provides reliable compressed speech-token generation while keeping the adaptation cost moderate. Scaling dialogue-adaptation data. Table 17 reports the results when varying the amount of speech-to-speech dialogue data, while fixing the pronunciation-adaptation data to 300h. The results show that using 50K dialogue examples provides strong balance between compression behavior and response quality. Therefore, we adopt 300h TTS data and 50K dialogue examples as the experimental configuration. C.4 Compression Across Data Sources and

sections.content: We randomly sample five queries from each of the 12 URO-Bench datasets, for 60 queries in total. Six evaluators rate the responses of Step-Audio 2 mini, matched Vanilla-FT, and CoSTA on 15 scale for speech fluency and semantic quality. This yields 60 3 6 = 1,080 response-level evaluations, each with two scores. Tables 19 and 20 report the means by dataset and language. For Figure 5, we compare the MOS scores given by the same evaluator to the same query for CoSTA and each baseline. higher, equal, or lower score counts as win, tie, or loss based on the MOS ratings. Each language/metric/baseline comparison therefore contains 30 6 = 180 paired scores. CoSTA has more wins than losses in every aggregate comparison, with ties forming the majority for fluency. The paired comparisons provide qualitative evidence of perceived quality preservation, while detailed task-level variations are reported in Appendix C.6. C.7 Detailed OpenS2S Transfer Results We adapt OpenS2S using vocabulary extension followed by both pronunciation and dialogue adaptation in each language. It retains its native GLM4-Voice tokenizer and speech decoder. Chinese evaluation uses AlpacaEval-zh, Claude-zh, and LCSTS-zh; English evaluation uses AlpacaEval, CommonEval, and Summary. The matched VanillaFT baselines use the corresponding adaptation data without BPE compression. Table 21 reports generated-token compression, ASR-CER for Chinese or ASR-WER for English, UTMOS, and GEval. CoSTA improves average content scores and alignment over matched fine-tuning while slightly lowering average UTMOS. sections.title: Extension
sections.content: Measurement setting. Vocabulary extension affects inference asymmetrically. The enlarged embedding table mainly increases parameter storage, while embedding lookup does not incur vocabularywide computation at each decoding step. In contrast, the LM head projects each hidden state over the full vocabulary, and the subsequent token selection also grows with vocabulary size. We therefore measure LM-head projection plus greedy argmax as the primary per-step computational overhead introduced by vocabulary extension. Transformer computation is excluded because its cost depends on the evolving prefix length, which itself changes with token compression and is therefore difficult to attribute to vocabulary extension alone. Table 24 reports the complete 0K320K measurements for S3Tokenizer V2 using identical BF16 hidden states on single A100 GPU at batch size 1, with median latency reported per step. Compression uses exact pooled token counts from the held-out Dialogue-ZH corpus in Figure 9; it is distinct from generated-token compression in Table 23. At 80K, the added output-projection rows contain 286.72M parameters and occupy 546.88 MiB in BF16. These storage figures cover the LM head alone. Compression versus per-step overhead. Let tM be the median projection-and-selection latency with added units and ρM the compression rate. We estimate the normalized output-layer cost for generating the same number of expanded speech tokens as Chead(M ) = ρM tM , (9) where ρM is represented as fraction. This estimate captures the isolated output-layer cost and excludes Transformer computation. At 80K, test compression is 62.29%, while per-step latency rises from 0.6902 to 1.0251 ms (+48.52%), yielding normalized cost of 0.925. At 160K, compression improves to 58.48%, but latency reaches 1.3598 ms (+97.01%), raising the normalized cost to 1.152. At 320K, compression reaches 54.94%, while latency increases to 2.0297 ms (+194.08%) and the normalized cost to 1.616. Thus, in this isolated measurement, continued compression gains eventually cease to offset the increasing per-step output-layer cost. Relation to full-model decoding. The isolated measurements characterize the additional outputlayer cost of vocabulary extension, but do not determine full-model efficiency. Token compression also reduces the number of Transformer decoding steps, an effect captured by the full-model experiments rather than by Chead. Indeed, AlpacaEval-zh decoding speed still increases slightly from 80K to 160K despite the higher normalized output-layer cost. Together, these results show why stronger compression does not necessarily translate into proportional full-model speedup and motivate considering compression, runtime, and response quality jointly when selecting vocabulary size. sections.title: E Case Study
sections.content: We present representative case studies selected from the English AlpacaEval and WildchatEval benchmarks. Case Studies 12 cover factual and commonsense questions, Case Study 3 illustrates sentence rewriting, Case Study 4 presents an openended dialogue, and Case Study 5 shows an empathetic customer-service reply. Across these cases, CoSTA generates compact speech-token sequences while preserving response quality; the generated BPE units are deterministically expanded back to the original speech-token space before waveform synthesis. These examples qualitatively demonstrate efficient compressed-token generation through token-space decoupling with the unchanged speech decoder.
